title: ST558 HW3
text:
Task 1: Conceptual Questions

If your working directory is myfolder/homework/, what relative path would you specify to get the file located at myfolder/MyData.csv?
Solution:
The relative path would be ../MyData.csv and ‘..’ is the parent folder.
What are the major benefits of using R projects?
Solution:
R Projects helps to keep files organized since each project has its own working directory and source doucments.This also make it easier to use relative paths.
What is Git and what is GitHub?
Solution:
Git is a tool that tracks the changes made to a file, whereas GitHub is a platform for storing and sharing Git projects
What are the two main differences between a tibble and a data.frame?
Solution:

Tibble has cleaner and more compact display when we print than dataframes. We can only see the data that is useful to us to see.
Tibble keeps the structure when selecting a single column, while a dataframe can turn the selected column to a vector.

Task 3: Combining Excel and Delimited Data

There is an excel version of the white wine data set available at https://www4.stat.ncsu.edu/~online/ datasets/white-wine.xlsx. • Download this file • Place it in a folder you know (such as your working directory for your project, the folder your .qmd file lives in, a data folder you’ve created in your repo, etc.) • Import the data from the first sheet using the readxl package • Print out the tibble (just call the object name)

When you print the data set out to the console, you may notice that some of the variable names are surrounded by backticks. This is because they are non-standard (they include a space in them). We can rename them in a number of ways. We’ll do it by reading in the variable names from the 2nd sheet of the same file. 3 • Read in the data from the 2nd sheet. This should return a data frame with one column containing alternative versions of the variable names. • Grab that column and overwrite the current column names (colnames()) of your white wine tibble. Note that colnames(object) allows for ‘left hand side assignment’. That is, you can call it on the left and store an object in it to overwrite it. Similar to names(object) <- c(…)
Solution:

Task 4: Writing a Function

Write a basic function (call it getIQR) that takes in a vector of numbers and returns the interquartile range (75th percentile - 25th percentile). You can use the quantile function. Remove the name on the returned vector (i.e. make sure the returned item doesn’t have a name like 75% or something like that). Allow your function to pass unnamed arguments to the quantile function.
Solution:

#Create IQR functions to calculate the range
getIQR <- function(x, ...) {
  q <- quantile(x, probs = c(0.25, 0.75), ...)
  unname(q[2] - q[1])
}

Take the object from question 7 and apply the getIRQ() function to the fixed_acidity and citric_acid columns (two function calls).
Solution:

#Calculate the IQR for fixed acidity and citric acid

getIQR(wine_data$fixed_acidity)

[1] 1.3

getIQR(wine_data$citric_acid)

[1] 0.14


Write another function (call it getCoefVar) that returns the sample coefficient of variation, defined as the sample standard deviation divided by the absolute value of the sample mean. Allow the function to pass unnamed arguments to sd and mean.
Solution:

#Function to calculate the coefficient of varaiation
getCoefVar<- function(x, ...){sd(x, ...)/abs(mean(x,...))}

Repeat question 9 using the getCoefVar() function.
Solution:

#Caluculating the coeff of variation for fixed acid and citric acid
getCoefVar(wine_data$fixed_acidity)

[1] 0.1796783

getCoefVar(wine_data$citric_acid)

[1] 0.4560663


Create a function (call it getSummaries) that takes in a vector and returns both the IQR and the coefficient of variation. Do not rewrite your above two functions, call them. When returning your values, give them appropriate names. (This would be called a wrapper function.)
Solution:

#Function that returns both IQR and coeff of variation
getSummaries<- function(x,...){c(IQR=getIQR(x,...), CoefVar=getCoefVar(x,...))}

4.)When you print the data set out to the console, you may notice that some of the variable names are surrounded by backticks. This is because they are non-standard (they include a space in them). We can rename them in a number of ways. We’ll do it by reading in the variable names from the 2nd sheet of the same file.
• Read in the data from the 2nd sheet. This should return a data frame with one column containing alternative versions of the variable names.
• Grab that column and overwrite the current column names (colnames()) of your white wine tibble. Note that colnames(object) allows for ‘left hand side assignment’. That is, you can call it on the left and store an object in it to overwrite it. Similar to names(object) <- c(…)

# get col names from the second sheet in white wine dataset

Task 4: Writing a Function
8.)Write a basic function (call it getIQR) that takes in a vector of numbers and returns the interquartile range (75th percentile - 25th percentile). You can use the quantile function. Remove the name on the returned vector (i.e. make sure the returned item doesn’t have a name like 75% or something like that). Allow your function to pass unnamed arguments to the quantile function

# function to get IQR range
getIQR <- function(x, ...) {
   quantile(x, probs = 0.75, names= FALSE, ...) - quantile(x, probs = .25, names= FALSE, ...)
  
}

9.) Take the object from question 7 and apply the getIRQ() function to the fixed_acidity and citric_acid columns (two function calls).

# call the function on fixed_acifity and citric_acid cols
getIQR(full_wine_df$fixed_acidity)

[1] 1.3

getIQR(full_wine_df$citric_acid)

[1] 0.14


10.)Write another function (call it getCoefVar) that returns the sample coefficient of variation, defined as the sample standard deviation divided by the absolute value of the sample mean. Allow the function to pass unnamed arguments to sd and mean.

# function that returns the sample coefficient of variation
getCoefVar <- function(x,...) {
  sd(x,...) / mean(x, ...)
}

11) Repeat question 9 using the getCoefVar() function

# call the getCoefVar for fixed_acidity and citric_acid cols
getCoefVar(full_wine_df$fixed_acidity)

[1] 0.1796783

getCoefVar(full_wine_df$citric_acid)

[1] 0.4560663


12.) Create a function (call it getSummaries) that takes in a vector and returns both the IQR and the coefficient of variation. Do not rewrite your above two functions, call them. When returning your values, give them appropriate names. (This would be called a wrapper function.)

# function that gets both the IQR and getCoefVar and returns both
getSummaries <- function(x) {
  cat("IQR: " , getIQR(x), "\n")
  cat("Coef Variance: " , getCoefVar(x), "\n")
}

13)Repeat question 2 with the getSummaries() function.
